skeleton.name: Skeleton (Whole)
skeleton.location: The complete internal framework of the body, from skull to toes.
skeleton.summary: The adult human skeleton is made of 206 bones divided into the axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs, sternum) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs, shoulder, and hip girdles). It gives the body shape, protects internal organs, and works with muscles to produce movement.
functions: Support — holds the body upright and gives it shape
Protection — shields organs like the brain, heart, and lungs
Movement — provides rigid levers for muscles to pull on
Mineral storage — stores calcium and phosphorus
Blood cell production — red bone marrow makes blood cells

skull.name: Skull
skull.location: The bony framework of the head, sitting atop the vertebral column.
skull.summary: The skull is made of many individually named bones (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid, and the facial bones) fused together at immovable joints called sutures. The upper part, the cranium, forms a rigid case around the brain.
functions: Encloses and protects the brain
Anchors the muscles of facial expression and chewing
Houses the eyes, ears, nose, and sense organs
Forms the upper jaw and the eye sockets

mandible.name: Mandible
mandible.location: The lower jawbone, the only movable bone of the skull.
mandible.summary: The mandible holds the lower teeth and forms a hinge joint with the temporal bone on each side (the temporomandibular joint), allowing the jaw to open, close, and grind.
functions: Anchors the lower teeth
Provides attachment for chewing muscles
Forms the temporomandibular joint with the skull

vertebral_column.name: Vertebral Column
vertebral_column.location: Runs from the base of the skull to the pelvis, along the midline of the back.
vertebral_column.summary: The spine is a stack of 33 vertebrae grouped into cervical (neck), thoracic (chest), lumbar (lower back), sacral, and coccygeal regions. Its gentle S-curve absorbs shock, and the hollow canal running through it protects the spinal cord.
functions: Supports the skull and trunk, transmitting body weight to the pelvis
Protects the spinal cord inside the vertebral canal
Allows the trunk to bend and twist
Anchors the ribs and back muscles

cervical_vertebrae.name: Cervical Vertebrae
cervical_vertebrae.location: The neck region of the spine, between the skull and the thoracic vertebrae — seven vertebrae labeled C1–C7.
cervical_vertebrae.summary: The smallest and most mobile vertebrae. The top two, the atlas (C1) and axis (C2), have a specialized shape that lets the head nod and rotate.
functions: Support the skull and allow it to nod and turn
Protect the upper spinal cord and vertebral arteries
Provide the neck's flexibility

thoracic_vertebrae.name: Thoracic Vertebrae
thoracic_vertebrae.location: The chest region of the spine, between the cervical and lumbar vertebrae — twelve vertebrae labeled T1–T12.
thoracic_vertebrae.summary: Each thoracic vertebra has facets where a pair of ribs attaches, making this region less mobile than the neck or lower back but central to forming the rib cage.
functions: Anchor point for all twelve pairs of ribs
Support the upper back and protect the mid-spinal cord
Help form the rib cage that protects the heart and lungs

lumbar_vertebrae.name: Lumbar Vertebrae
lumbar_vertebrae.location: The lower back region of the spine, between the thoracic vertebrae and the sacrum — five vertebrae labeled L1–L5.
lumbar_vertebrae.summary: The largest, sturdiest vertebrae, built to bear most of the body's weight. This is also the most common site of lower back pain and disc problems.
functions: Bear the majority of the upper body's weight
Allow bending and twisting of the lower back
Protect the lowest part of the spinal cord and cauda equina

sacrum.name: Sacrum
sacrum.location: A triangular bone at the base of the spine, wedged between the two hip bones.
sacrum.summary: Formed from five fused vertebrae, the sacrum transfers the weight of the upper body to the pelvis and legs, and forms the back wall of the pelvic cavity.
functions: Connects the spine to the pelvis
Transfers body weight from the spine to the legs
Anchors pelvic floor and lower back muscles

sternum.name: Sternum
sternum.location: A flat bone in the center of the chest, in front of the heart.
sternum.summary: The breastbone has three parts — the manubrium, body, and xiphoid process — and anchors the ribs at the front via costal cartilage, completing the protective rib cage.
functions: Anchors the ribs at the front of the chest
Shields the heart and major vessels
Provides attachment for chest muscles

ribs.name: Ribs
ribs.location: Twelve curved pairs of bones forming a cage around the chest, attached to the thoracic vertebrae at the back and mostly to the sternum at the front.
ribs.summary: The rib cage is a flexible, protective enclosure: the top seven pairs attach directly to the sternum, the next three attach indirectly through cartilage, and the bottom two pairs ("floating ribs") attach only to the spine.
functions: Protect the heart and lungs
Expand and contract with breathing muscles to change chest volume
Support the shoulder girdle muscles

clavicle_left.name: Left Clavicle
clavicle_left.location: The collarbone, running horizontally between the sternum and the left shoulder.
clavicle_left.summary: A slender, S-shaped bone that braces the shoulder away from the body, letting the arm swing freely.
functions: Connects the arm to the trunk via the sternum
Braces the shoulder joint
Protects underlying nerves and blood vessels

clavicle_right.name: Right Clavicle
clavicle_right.location: The collarbone, running horizontally between the sternum and the right shoulder.
clavicle_right.summary: A slender, S-shaped bone that braces the shoulder away from the body, letting the arm swing freely.
functions: Connects the arm to the trunk via the sternum
Braces the shoulder joint
Protects underlying nerves and blood vessels

scapula_left.name: Left Scapula
scapula_left.location: The left shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the rib cage.
scapula_left.summary: The scapula glides over the rib cage and forms the socket half of the shoulder joint, giving the arm an unusually wide range of motion.
functions: Forms the shoulder joint with the humerus
Anchors many shoulder and back muscles
Allows the shoulder to rotate and glide

scapula_right.name: Right Scapula
scapula_right.location: The right shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the rib cage.
scapula_right.summary: The scapula glides over the rib cage and forms the socket half of the shoulder joint, giving the arm an unusually wide range of motion.
functions: Forms the shoulder joint with the humerus
Anchors many shoulder and back muscles
Allows the shoulder to rotate and glide

humerus_left.name: Left Humerus
humerus_left.location: The single bone of the left upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow.
humerus_left.summary: The longest bone of the arm. Its rounded head fits into the scapula's shallow socket at the shoulder, and its lower end forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna.
functions: Forms the shoulder joint with the scapula
Forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna
Anchors major arm muscles like the biceps and triceps

humerus_right.name: Right Humerus
humerus_right.location: The single bone of the right upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow.
humerus_right.summary: The longest bone of the arm. Its rounded head fits into the scapula's shallow socket at the shoulder, and its lower end forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna.
functions: Forms the shoulder joint with the scapula
Forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna
Anchors major arm muscles like the biceps and triceps

radius_left.name: Left Radius
radius_left.location: One of two forearm bones, on the thumb side of the left forearm.
radius_left.summary: The radius rotates around the ulna, which is what lets you turn your palm face-up or face-down.
functions: Forms part of the elbow and wrist joints
Rotates to turn the palm up or down (pronation/supination)

radius_right.name: Right Radius
radius_right.location: One of two forearm bones, on the thumb side of the right forearm.
radius_right.summary: The radius rotates around the ulna, which is what lets you turn your palm face-up or face-down.
functions: Forms part of the elbow and wrist joints
Rotates to turn the palm up or down (pronation/supination)

ulna_left.name: Left Ulna
ulna_left.location: One of two forearm bones, on the little-finger side of the left forearm.
ulna_left.summary: The ulna is the main hinge partner for the elbow — its curved notch locks around the humerus so the elbow only bends and straightens, rather than wobbling side to side.
functions: Forms the main hinge of the elbow joint
Anchors forearm muscles
Provides a stable axis for the radius to rotate around

ulna_right.name: Right Ulna
ulna_right.location: One of two forearm bones, on the little-finger side of the right forearm.
ulna_right.summary: The ulna is the main hinge partner for the elbow — its curved notch locks around the humerus so the elbow only bends and straightens, rather than wobbling side to side.
functions: Forms the main hinge of the elbow joint
Anchors forearm muscles
Provides a stable axis for the radius to rotate around

hand_bones.name: Bones of the Hand
hand_bones.location: The wrist and hand, at the end of the forearm.
hand_bones.summary: Each hand has 27 bones: eight small carpal (wrist) bones, five metacarpal bones forming the palm, and fourteen phalanges forming the fingers and thumb.
functions: Carpals form a flexible, shock-absorbing wrist
Metacarpals form the framework of the palm
Phalanges give fingers their fine, precise movement

pelvis_left.name: Left Hip Bone
pelvis_left.location: The left half of the pelvic girdle, connecting the spine to the left leg.
pelvis_left.summary: Also called the os coxae, each hip bone is actually three bones (ilium, ischium, and pubis) fused together. Together with the sacrum, the two hip bones form the bowl-shaped pelvis.
functions: Connects the spine to the lower limb
Supports body weight while standing and walking
Protects pelvic organs
Forms the hip joint with the femur

pelvis_right.name: Right Hip Bone
pelvis_right.location: The right half of the pelvic girdle, connecting the spine to the right leg.
pelvis_right.summary: Also called the os coxae, each hip bone is actually three bones (ilium, ischium, and pubis) fused together. Together with the sacrum, the two hip bones form the bowl-shaped pelvis.
functions: Connects the spine to the lower limb
Supports body weight while standing and walking
Protects pelvic organs
Forms the hip joint with the femur

femur_left.name: Left Femur
femur_left.location: The single bone of the left thigh, between the hip and the knee.
femur_left.summary: The longest, strongest bone in the body. Its rounded head fits into the hip socket, and its lower end forms the knee joint with the tibia.
functions: Forms the hip joint with the pelvis
Forms the knee joint with the tibia and patella
Bears the body's weight while standing and walking

femur_right.name: Right Femur
femur_right.location: The single bone of the right thigh, between the hip and the knee.
femur_right.summary: The longest, strongest bone in the body. Its rounded head fits into the hip socket, and its lower end forms the knee joint with the tibia.
functions: Forms the hip joint with the pelvis
Forms the knee joint with the tibia and patella
Bears the body's weight while standing and walking

patella_left.name: Left Patella
patella_left.location: The kneecap, sitting in front of the left knee joint.
patella_left.summary: The largest sesamoid bone in the body — a bone embedded within a tendon (the quadriceps tendon) rather than connected directly to other bones at a joint.
functions: Protects the front of the knee joint
Increases the leverage of the thigh muscles when straightening the knee

patella_right.name: Right Patella
patella_right.location: The kneecap, sitting in front of the right knee joint.
patella_right.summary: The largest sesamoid bone in the body — a bone embedded within a tendon (the quadriceps tendon) rather than connected directly to other bones at a joint.
functions: Protects the front of the knee joint
Increases the leverage of the thigh muscles when straightening the knee

tibia_left.name: Left Tibia
tibia_left.location: The shin bone — the larger of the two lower-leg bones, on the inner side of the left leg.
tibia_left.summary: The tibia carries almost all of the body's weight below the knee; the thinner fibula alongside it mainly provides muscle attachment and ankle stability.
functions: Bears most of the body's weight below the knee
Forms the knee joint with the femur
Forms the ankle joint with the foot bones

tibia_right.name: Right Tibia
tibia_right.location: The shin bone — the larger of the two lower-leg bones, on the inner side of the right leg.
tibia_right.summary: The tibia carries almost all of the body's weight below the knee; the thinner fibula alongside it mainly provides muscle attachment and ankle stability.
functions: Bears most of the body's weight below the knee
Forms the knee joint with the femur
Forms the ankle joint with the foot bones

fibula_left.name: Left Fibula
fibula_left.location: The thinner of the two lower-leg bones, on the outer side of the left leg.
fibula_left.summary: Unlike the tibia, the fibula carries very little body weight. Instead it stabilizes the ankle and provides a long attachment surface for lower-leg muscles.
functions: Stabilizes the ankle joint
Anchors lower-leg muscles
Provides a small contribution to the knee joint

fibula_right.name: Right Fibula
fibula_right.location: The thinner of the two lower-leg bones, on the outer side of the right leg.
fibula_right.summary: Unlike the tibia, the fibula carries very little body weight. Instead it stabilizes the ankle and provides a long attachment surface for lower-leg muscles.
functions: Stabilizes the ankle joint
Anchors lower-leg muscles
Provides a small contribution to the knee joint

foot_bones.name: Bones of the Foot
foot_bones.location: The ankle and foot, at the end of the lower leg.
foot_bones.summary: Each foot has 26 bones: seven tarsal bones (including the heel bone, the calcaneus, and the ankle bone, the talus), five metatarsal bones forming the sole, and fourteen phalanges forming the toes.
functions: Tarsals form the ankle and the arches of the foot
Metatarsals and the arches absorb impact while walking and running
Phalanges give the toes balance and push-off power
